introduction-why-http11-wasnt-enough.core: HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, so a slow response blocks those behind it (head-of-line blocking). Browsers worked around it by opening about 6 connections per host, domain sharding, sprite sheets and bundling, and every request repeats verbose text headers. Modern pages with 100+ resources made those hacks costly, which motivated HTTP/2's multiplexing and HTTP/3's move to QUIC.

first_principles.problem: A page with 120 assets loads slowly despite a fast connection because requests queue behind each other.
truths: One request at a time per connection blocks.
Extra connections cost handshakes and congestion state.

analogy.title: A single-lane drive-through
analogy.story: One slow order holds up every car behind it, so restaurants open more lanes, which is expensive.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Latency dominated by queuing, not bandwidth.

check.q: Why did browsers open ~6 connections per host under HTTP/1.1?
check.a: To parallelise requests, because each connection could only carry one request/response at a time.

http2-the-multiplexing-revolution.core: HTTP/2 keeps HTTP semantics but changes the wire format to binary frames. Many concurrent streams share one TCP connection, interleaved frame by frame, so a slow response doesn't block others at the HTTP layer. A single connection per origin means one TLS handshake and better congestion behaviour, and old hacks like domain sharding become counterproductive.

first_principles.problem: After enabling HTTP/2, domain sharding now hurts performance by preventing connection reuse.

analogy.title: A multi-lane motorway merged into one road with numbered cars
analogy.story: Cars from different trips share the road, each tagged so they reassemble at the destination.
analogy.breaks: Cars can change lanes; a lost TCP packet still blocks all streams (TCP HOL).

check.q: What problem does HTTP/2 not solve?
check.a: TCP-level head-of-line blocking: a lost packet stalls all streams on the connection until retransmitted.

http2-hpack-header-compression-and-serve.core: HPACK compresses headers using a static table of common headers, a dynamic table of headers seen on this connection, and Huffman encoding. Repeated headers such as cookies shrink to a byte or two, and it was designed to resist the CRIME-style attacks that broke gzip-compressed headers. Server push let servers send resources before they were requested, but it was rarely beneficial and browsers removed support; 103 Early Hints replaced it.

first_principles.problem: Mobile requests carry 2 KB of repeated cookies and headers each, wasting bandwidth on slow links.
truths: Compression state can be shared per connection.
Pushing unrequested data often wastes bandwidth.

analogy.title: Shorthand between regular correspondents
analogy.story: After the first letter, 'as before' replaces the whole address block.
analogy.breaks: Shorthand can be guessed; HPACK avoids compression oracles by design.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Browser starts fetching CSS/JS while HTML is generated.

code.text:
HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </app.css>; rel=preload; as=style
Link: </app.js>; rel=preload; as=script

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

check.q: Why was HTTP/2 server push removed from browsers?
check.a: It often pushed resources already cached or not needed, wasting bandwidth, with little measured benefit.

http3-solving-the-tcp-problem.core: HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics onto QUIC (over UDP). Each stream recovers from loss independently, removing TCP's head-of-line blocking; TLS 1.3 is built into the handshake (1-RTT, 0-RTT resumption); connection IDs let connections survive network changes; and QPACK replaces HPACK to tolerate out-of-order streams. Servers advertise it via Alt-Svc, and clients fall back to HTTP/2 if UDP is blocked.

first_principles.problem: On lossy mobile networks, HTTP/2 pages stall because one lost TCP packet blocks every stream.
truths: TCP orders all bytes on a connection.
UDP can be blocked, so fallback is needed.

analogy.title: Separate couriers per parcel instead of one truck
analogy.story: If one parcel is delayed, the others still arrive on time.
analogy.breaks: Couriers are independent companies; QUIC streams share congestion control.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clients upgrade to h3; fall back to h2 if UDP blocked.

check.q: How does a browser learn a site supports HTTP/3?
check.a: Via the Alt-Svc response header (or an HTTPS DNS record) advertising h3, then it tries QUIC on later requests.

grpc-and-protocol-buffers-binary-contrac.core: Protocol Buffers define messages and services in a .proto schema; code generators produce typed clients and servers in many languages. The binary encoding uses field numbers instead of names, so it's compact and fast, and backward and forward compatibility come from rules: never reuse field numbers, add new optional fields, and reserve removed ones. The schema is the contract between teams.

first_principles.problem: JSON APIs between services break silently when one team renames a field.
truths: Field numbers decouple names from wire format.

analogy.title: A numbered form
analogy.story: Box 7 is always 'postcode', even if the label text changes, and new boxes are added at the end.
analogy.breaks: Paper forms can't be auto-validated; protobuf generates typed code.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Old clients ignore field 4; renaming fields is safe.

check.q: Why must you never reuse a protobuf field number?
check.a: Old clients/data would interpret the new field's bytes as the old field, corrupting meaning.

grpc-high-performance-service-to-service.core: gRPC runs protobuf services over HTTP/2: unary calls plus client, server and bidirectional streaming on one multiplexed connection, with deadlines, cancellation and metadata built in. Because connections are long-lived, L4 load balancers pin all calls to one backend, so use L7 (Envoy, a service mesh) or client-side balancing. Use gRPC-Web or a gateway for browsers.

first_principles.problem: After moving to gRPC, one backend pod gets all traffic because the L4 load balancer balances connections, not requests.
derivation: Use **unary and streaming** RPCs as fit.

analogy.title: A dedicated phone line between offices
analogy.story: Once connected, all calls flow over that line, so a switchboard that only routes new lines never spreads the load.
analogy.breaks: Phone lines carry one call at a time; HTTP/2 multiplexes many.

check.q: Why does gRPC often need L7 load balancing?
check.a: Calls are multiplexed on long-lived connections, so connection-level (L4) balancing sends all requests from a client to one backend.
